beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: AI security is a rapidly evolving field, and organisations of every size are working out how best to approach it.
beats.got: You can't judge safety from the output, so you run a check. The second paragraph is filler.

beats.trigger: The Module 4 prework adds two reads: (1) personal skills as the package format that carries expertise into your agent
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a reading list, and I haven't done the reading.

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (prompt injection direct and indirect, secrets-in-context, tool-confusion, skill supply-chain)
beats.got: A list of jargon. No cost or payback anywhere in it. 'Residual risk' is the only term I recognise.

beats.trigger: Name the thing you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: This is a fair question. My answer: who is accountable when it's wrong, and where does the data go?

beats.trigger: A tool call is not a new species of work. It is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent writes text and the runtime turns it into an action. That's how it can be misled. Useful but abstract.

beats.trigger: Industry analysts expect agent adoption to accelerate significantly over the coming years, which makes it all the more important to think about governance now.
beats.got: Nothing. It's a brochure paragraph with no source and no figure. The first two paragraphs were fine.

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: The attack is plain English inside a document the agent reads, and my existing controls don't see it. That is a risk I'd have to raise myself.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (break it into two agents with different trust levels).
beats.got: There are five mitigations, and scope and gate are cheap and make sense. I can picture an approval step on a payment.

beats.trigger: Accept the residual on record, or close the door.
beats.got: This is how I already handle risk: a register, an owner, and accept or close. The 'hope it doesn't happen' line is fair.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: The point is you never reach certainty, so you run the loop again. I agree, but I want a cadence and an owner.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent can load and use.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable checklist the agent loads. It's like a procedure document. Forty minutes, though.

beats.trigger: The raw run shows which rules can be checked from files and which ones need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The agent read our policy files and sorted the rules into checkable and not checkable. That's close to a control test, and I like it.

beats.trigger: The customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript.
beats.got: I type three to five lines of what matters, such as finance data and customer names. It asked me, which is fine.

beats.trigger: You'll get a lot of questions. The grill is wide on purpose: the agent probes both lenses and won't stop at one round.
beats.got: A long question round. I'd answer a few and hand off the rest.

beats.trigger: "You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."
beats.got: I can delegate the rest after answering what I know. That's efficient, and I finished early.

beats.trigger: This task interface can't write into your runtime's personal directories.
beats.got: Save mechanics vary by tool and are fiddly. IT would have to approve this on finance data.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: I have a reusable check. Agent controls add to ours and don't replace them. Fair.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: This is an honest framing. I'm going to get a ranked list, not a pass.

beats.trigger: Type `/` in the prompt and look for `/security-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: Check that the skill loaded. Technical housekeeping.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The report found gaps I hadn't thought of and marked several rows 'I can't tell'. That's a deliverable I can show someone.

beats.trigger: You now have the assessment half of the loop.
beats.got: A ranked risk report, with each risk explained in my own system's terms. It's close to what I'd expect from internal audit, in minutes.

beats.trigger: A mitigation reduces, it does not eliminate.
beats.got: I picked one risk, the agent applied a fix, and the report shows the residual I accept on record. This is the closest thing to a figure I can defend.

beats.trigger: You must do the work.
beats.got: Production needs more risk control than one mitigation. It's vague and doesn't say how much work.

beats.trigger: The unease stays. Nothing today resolves it. That's the curriculum.
beats.got: The agent writes rules into the instructions file for future sessions. The closing paragraph repeats the boilerplate from the start.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: A skill is a shareable procedure, like a template. This could work for month-end variance commentary.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: Four sound takeaways. The last one is what I'd tell the board.

beats.trigger: Come to Module 5 without the two missing-check sentences and you'll be reconstructing them while the benchmark is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework: one sentence per case on the missing check. Fine, if I do it.

beats.trigger: what check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two cases, a lawyer and a Big Four report. Those are real consequences, not hypotheticals. I'd read them.

take_homes: An agent's output can't tell me whether it's safe. I need a repeatable check that runs, and some rows will stay 'I can't tell'.
Risk is loop-shaped: assess, apply one mitigation, name the residual, then accept it on record or close the door. That is the same register discipline I already run, applied to agents.
The attack is plain English inside a document the agent reads, so a firewall won't catch it. Scope, split, filter, gate and review are the controls, and they sit on top of ours.

monday.move: Ask my controller to run the packaged security check against the month-end variance agent, read the residual list, and put it to IT as the basis for approving finance data.
monday.when: Within two weeks, once IT has said what they'll allow
monday.stop_condition: IT refuses the tool for finance data, or the residual risk comes out as unacceptable.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, and I don't know what a licence costs per month for 40 people.

misconception.why: I came in thinking AI is a licence you buy. The module showed me the risk sits in how the organisation sets scope, gates and checks the agent, so it is a capability you build and keep running. I'm not fully changed, because nobody put a cost on it.

one_line: Good on risk discipline, and the audit exercise gave me a ranked list and a residual I could take to the board, but cut the brochure paragraphs and put a price on it.
